#5438. After 7 Years and 99% Speed Leap, Solana (SOL) Finally Drops Its 'Beta' Label

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation said.

Solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status."

The Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

According to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once."

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

#5437. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

Shiba Inu fell to a rare low of $0.0000037 as cryptocurrencies tumbled over the weekend. This low marked the lowest seen in years, going back to 2021, as it fell below the $0.000004 level, which has served as support since the start of 2026.

Last week’s bruising selloff following a tougher interest-rate outlook and a risk-off mood deepened the gloom around the cryptocurrency.

Shiba Inu fell for four straight days in the past week, dropping to a low of $0.0000037 on November 14, 2026, coinciding with the first death cross on its daily chart in 2026.

At the time of writing, Shiba Inu was down 3.36% in the last 24 hours to $0.00000386 as the crypto market selloff intensified, with a total of $203.7 million liquidated. Mazrael, a long-time Shiba Inu community member and SHIB developer, reacted to the token's latest price weakness with a simple message: "1 SHIB is always 1 SHIB" in response to an X user who pointed out Shiba Inu's price drop.

The phrase, often used in the context of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies during price downturns, serves as a reminder to focus on the unit itself rather than short-term fiat volatility. While a single coin always counts as one unit of the network, the argument against this saying is that fiat value changes amid volatility.

Fed Chairman Kelvin Warsh is set to speak later on Monday on the impact of technology on productivity and jobs, potentially triggering volatility in the markets. The Federal Reserve’s minutes from its October meeting, where it left rates unchanged, will be released Wednesday. Markets have largely priced in a quarter percentage point hike in December.

While the Shiba Inu price is trading in the red, the SHIB burn rate is up 1922%, with 136.81 million SHIB sent to dead wallets in the last 24 hours.

155.03 million SHIB have been burned in the last seven days, with the weekly burn rate up 14.40%. 395.10 million SHIB worth $1753 was burned in the last 30 days, although the burn rate was down 55.45% in the time frame.

A total of 410,845,352,742,359 SHIB has been burned in 21,967 transactions, contributing to 41.08% of the total supply.

Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, spent $228.1 million buying back its STRC preferred stock between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, according to the company's new filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Over the same period, Strategy bought 485 BTC for $33.4 million, so the company spent almost seven times more on STRC than on Bitcoin.

"Strategy has acquired 485 BTC and repurchased $228M of STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets," Michael Saylor wrote on X.

The filing shows that Strategy sold 2.09 million shares of its Class A common stock and raised $244.7 million. The company used $206.3 million of that amount for STRC buybacks and added another $21.8 million from interest earned on its dollar reserves.

The 485 BTC were bought at an average price of $68,887 per coin. The remaining $5 million from the share sales stayed on the books as free cash.

STRC, also known as Stretch, is a perpetual preferred stock with a variable monthly dividend, and Strategy launched it in July 2025.

When the price of Bitcoin slipped below $65,000, STRC fell to $99.08. Strategy aims to keep STRC close to its $100 par value, and the company has another $332.2 million set aside for buybacks. The board of Strategy also approved a December STRC dividend at an annual rate of 12%, or $1.00 per share.

"USD Duration is 3.4 yrs and STRC's BTC Credit tightened to 67 bps (-3 bps), assuming 10% BTC ARR, 40% BTC Vol, and a BTC price of $68,800," Saylor added.

As of Nov. 15, Strategy held 850,849 BTC, bought for a total of $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. On Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $63,941, and Strategy's holdings are worth around $54.4 billion.

The unrealized loss of the company on its Bitcoin holdings stands at around $9.8 billion. On Sunday, when the price of Bitcoin fell to $62,029 on Bitfinex, the loss was above $11 billion.

Strategy also holds $4.9 billion in dollar assets, and $4.75 billion of that amount is in its dedicated USD reserve.

#5434. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5433. US and Canada Announce Massive Crypto Fraud Crackdown

Authorities in the United States and Canada have announced a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) announced on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," said Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

#5432. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5431. Ripple’s Brad Garlinghouse Says Crypto Markets Could Rebound After Anthropic Goes Public

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse believes the recent crypto market sell-off stems largely from investors rotating capital into high-profile initial public offerings. The Ripple boss and crypto billionaire anticipates a recovery once Anthropic’s massive listing is fully absorbed.

Speaking to CNBC on November 19th, Garlinghouse drew a direct parallel to SpaceX’s public debut earlier in the year. He explained that when major IPOs generate intense demand, investors often sell liquid assets such as Bitcoin and XRP to free up cash for share subscriptions.

The same pattern, he said, unfolded ahead of Anthropic’s offering. After SpaceX completed its listing, crypto markets staged a notable rebound. Garlinghouse expects a similar bounce this time.

Anthropic, the artificial-intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot family, has priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the previously marketed range of $70 to $78.

The deal ranks among the largest IPOs in history, raising tens of billions of dollars and valuing the company in the trillion-dollar range, and shares are set to begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Such blockbuster offerings typically attract enormous institutional and retail interest, temporarily diverting capital from other risk assets. Once the primary allocation is complete and secondary-market trading stabilizes, some of that capital often flows back into crypto and other liquid markets.

Bitcoin had slipped near $62,000 on Wednesday before recovering above $63,000 early Thursday. Garlinghouse framed the dip as a temporary capital-rotation effect rather than a fundamental loss of confidence in digital assets. He also expressed confidence that Anthropic’s shares would trade strongly given the strong demand and pricing above the range.

Looking further ahead, Garlinghouse remained optimistic about blockchain’s long-term role. He predicted that within roughly a decade, blockchain technology will be deeply embedded across global financial infrastructure, much as artificial intelligence has already transformed multiple industries.

His comments highlight how large technology IPOs can create short-term pressure on crypto while potentially reinforcing longer-term narratives around innovation and capital markets.

#5430. Canada’s National Bank Discloses XRP Position Through Bitwise

Despite the slowed performance witnessed across the XRP ETF market in recent weeks, it appears that interest in the investment product remains intact especially through its largest issuer, Bitwise.

In a recent 13F filings with the U.S. SEC, the national bank of Canada, revealed it recently joined the XRP ETF ecosystem, showcasing its exposure to XRP through the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Although the bank did not disclose the specific amount it had invested in the asset, the filing has triggered discussions as it highlights XRP’s growing exposure among institutional investors.

Notably, the Form 13F the bank filed with the SEC covers the third quarter of 2026, which ended on September 30. This suggests that it had recently joined the XRP ecosystem despite the prolonged market weakness.

Unlike regular investors who purchase XRP directly from exchanges and hold in their wallets, the bank invested in XRP through Bitwise's fund.

With its XRP ETF offering, Bitwise allows traditional investors to gain exposure to XRP without having to manage the crypto asset themselves.

Although XRP has continued to see major institutions and banks join its ETF ecosystem, participation in the XRP funds have slowed significantly following the ongoing market volatility.

While the exposure showcased by the major Canadian bank shows growing XRP ETF adoption, it doesn’t change the fact that institutional traders are beginning to take caution as they have just recorded the highest weekly withdrawals since March 2026.

The bank’s XRP exposure has triggered discussions as it shows that it has retained its position till September 30 despite the persisting market correction.

On Thursday alone, the day Anthropic listed on Nasdaq, the S&P 500 fell 2% for its sixth straight loss, and BTC slipped under $62,000.

BREAKING: US technology stock valuations have hit their lowest level since March 2020 amid the market correction.The S&P 500 Info Tech Index P/E ratio is now at its lowest since March 20th, 2020, at 16.4x. pic.twitter.com/KMxsZxBlql

The two markets are falling in step, and that wasn’t always the case. We measured how closely BTC and the Nasdaq have moved day to day since 2015. For its first years, Bitcoin went its own way. Since 2020, it has traded more and more like a tech stock, and over the past 40 trading days the link has been stronger than in any full calendar year.

So which stocks are hurting most, and why does crypto now fall with them?

We checked how 45 large AI, chip and crypto-related stocks have done since the October 6 peak. The worst performers fall into a few groups, and most of them sit right where AI and crypto overlap:

The biggest names held up far better. Microsoft is down 6%, Tesla 2%, Amazon is flat and Apple is up 5%.

Nvidia is at the center of the AI slide. CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week amid a personal scandal, and the chipmaker has lost $735 billion in market value since it broke, the Associated Press reported. Worries that AI stocks had run too high added to the pressure. So did new US limits on remote access to advanced chips and talk of curbs on new data centers after this month’s midterm elections. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said.

Rates aren’t helping either. The 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%, and inflation is running at 3.1%.

To answer whether crypto and stocks always moved together, we compared BTC’s daily price changes with those of the Nasdaq Composite, year by year since 2015. The measure, called correlation, runs from 1 (always moving together) to 0 (no link) and -1 (always moving in opposite directions).

So the answer is no. Crypto and stocks didn’t always move together. It’s a habit that started in 2020 and has grown stronger this year.

Several changes since 2020 explain why Bitcoin now trades like a risky tech stock:

That last group shows the link most clearly. When AI shares fell, the miners that rent space to AI firms fell harder than either the coin or Nvidia.

As long as Bitcoin keeps moving with the Nasdaq, the next clue for BTC may come from tech stocks, starting with Nvidia. A calmer week for AI shares would give $58,500 a better chance to hold. Another leg down in tech would likely drag crypto with it.

Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab announced new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

Nvidia released a new decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the company, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia said that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing."

Nvidia and IBM also announced plans for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform."

In 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

#5426. Harvard Refuses to Dump Bitcoin Holdings Despite Downturn

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

As per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

The Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#5425. Lagarde Sees a €23 Billion Opportunity: Can Tokenization Finally Unite Europe’s 27 Markets?

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde said on Friday, November 20, that tokenization could give Europe something it has chased for decades: one market for financial assets instead of 27. She warned that the chance may not last, because the market is growing fast and its rules are still being written.

JUST IN: 🇪🇺 ECB President Christine Lagarde says tokenization could create a unified European market for digital assets.

She made the case in a keynote at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress. She told the room it was her eighth speech there as ECB President, and her last.

Tokenization means issuing assets such as bonds, shares or fund units as digital tokens on a blockchain, where they can be traded and settled in one place. Europe’s own digital money, though, is still tiny next to the dollar’s. We compared euro and dollar stablecoins to see how far behind it is.

Discover: Bitcoin Falls With Stocks Again: A Link That Only Began in 2020 Is Getting Tighter

Lagarde spent most of the speech on why Europe acts too late on slow-moving problems. Tokenization was one of three areas where she said the ECB had tried to act early. The other two were the digital euro and the euro’s role abroad.

“With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity,” she said in the speech published by the ECB.

The catch is timing. Lagarde said the global market for tokenized assets was worth around €23 billion in March, five times its size a year earlier. As it grows, its standards will set.

She warned that if standards develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. Europe’s stock and bond markets already work that way, with separate national systems that have proved very hard to merge.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The ECB has already built part of the plumbing. In September, it launched Pontes, a link that lets tokenized trades settle in central bank money, the safest form of money there is, on Eurosystem systems. Every platform can now use the same settlement asset.

Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism, the euro area’s rescue fund, settled a €1 billion bond issued directly as a token on Pontes.

A second project, Appia, is working with banks and other firms on common standards for an integrated European market. But Lagarde said the central bank cannot finish the job alone. “Infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators,” she said.

Stablecoins are tokens pegged to a currency, and they are the cash leg of most crypto and tokenized trades today. On that front, Europe is far behind.

Dollar stablecoins in circulation total about $283.7 billion, while euro stablecoins total about $815 million. That is $1 in euro tokens for every $348 in dollar tokens, or a 0.29% share.

The euro side is growing faster from its small base. Since the stablecoin rules in the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) law took effect on June 30, 2024, euro stablecoins have grown 244%, while dollar stablecoins grew 76%. That doubled the euro’s share, from 0.15% to 0.29%.

One issuer dominates. Circle’s EURC accounts for about 62% of the euro total, ahead of SG-Forge’s EURCV.

This is why the ECB wants tokenized trades in Europe to settle in central bank money rather than in private tokens. In a market run on dollar stablecoins, European tokenization would depend on a currency the ECB does not control.

#5424. Ripple's Schwartz Reveals Why XRP Ledger Used Satoshi's Code

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet said that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating new ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," said Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz said it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

"It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz said.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5419. Selling Pressure Mounts as Bitcoin Whales Dump $3.4 Billion in BTC

Bitcoin (BTC) is facing renewed selling pressure as large holders continue to reduce their exposure, with on-chain data showing that whales have redistributed about $3.4 billion worth of the cryptocurrency over the past two weeks.

Notably, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has fallen nearly 13% over the past week. The decline extends its November losses, bringing its price to a three-month low.

According to analyst Ali Martinez, large entities have sold or redistributed 48,618 BTC, valued at approximately $3.4 billion, over the past two weeks.

“Whales are still reducing their exposure. The selling hasn’t stopped yet,” Martinez tweeted.

The continued distribution suggests that major holders are yet to regain confidence in Bitcoin’s near-term prospects. With thousands of coins changing hands, the market faces the challenge of absorbing this supply without triggering further downward pressure.

Beyond whale activity, Bitcoin’s weekly performance is adding to concerns about the market’s strength.

Analyst Ted Pillows noted that the cryptocurrency has closed six consecutive weeks in the red, a pattern previously seen during bear markets. Trading below both moving averages further weakens its recovery prospects.

“Along with that, Bitcoin failed to hold both the 200W EMA and 200W MA, which is a major sign of weakness. As long as BTC stays below these levels, sellers are in full control,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, several important price levels have given way, leaving Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline.

Mookie, an advocate at Bitget Wallet and ambassador at Dinari Global, highlighted the cryptocurrency’s failure to maintain successive support levels, warning that $57,700 could come into focus if buyers fail to regain control.

“If BTC can’t get back above $66.5K. we could see another drop toward the July low at $57.7K. But if buyers push it back above $66.5K we might finally see a bounce. Still not convinced we’re done dropping,” he noted.

His comments put $66,500 at the center of Bitcoin’s immediate price outlook. Reclaiming that level could help buyers regain some momentum, while another rejection would leave the July low of $57,700 as a potential downside target.

Despite the prevailing bearish sentiment, some market observers believe Bitcoin could be approaching a turning point.

Gordon, founder of Crypto Crib and co-founder of Alphametrics, pointed to a potential inverse head-and-shoulders formation, suggesting that extreme pessimism could set the stage for a reversal.

“All longs have been wiped out, sentiment is max bearish, and retail is going heavy short. This is where reversal happens,” he commented.

An inverse head-and-shoulders pattern is a technical formation often associated with a potential bullish reversal after an extended decline. It typically consists of three troughs, with the middle one forming the lowest point.

Gordon’s assessment offers a contrasting view to the warnings from other analysts. He believes that widespread bearish positioning and the liquidation of leveraged long positions could create conditions for buyers to return.

However, the formation does not guarantee an immediate recovery. Bitcoin still needs enough buying interest to reverse its recent losses and reclaim key price levels.

At press time, BTC was trading at $59,299, down 5.40% over the past 24 hours.

#5418. Mastercard Spotlights XRP Ledger After Groundbreaking Test

After an important hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore new possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI

Global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

The hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

One of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the company's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

#5417. CFTC Makes Historic Move With Blockchain Derivatives Approval

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

On Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He said that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

Selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

For some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

The latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

#5416. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5415. Major Crypto-Stealing Exploit in JavaScript Emerges: Zoom, CNN, HSBC Affected

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing users multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

According to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

If successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

#5414. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

This is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake said.

According to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes recently named NEAR among four tokens that he expects to rise before the end of the AI bubble. Hayes set targets of $6 for NEAR, $2,800 for ETH, $1,800 for ZEC, and $40 for VVV.

"The size is small to medium as conviction is meh, but if the music is playing, you gotta dance," Hayes wrote on X.

The Four Horsemen shall pump and then usher in the end of the AI bubble: $ETH = $2800 $ZEC = $1800 $NEAR = $6.00 $VVV = $40 The size is small to medium as conviction is meh, but if the music playing you gotta dance.

Total volume through NEAR Intents, the cross-chain liquidity layer of the protocol, has reached $39 billion, and the service was recently integrated into Talos OEMS, an institutional trading platform.

Ledger, a crypto wallet firm, said it had experienced a security incident related to Optimizely, a third-party service used on its official website, but reassured its users about the security of their devices and private keys.

In a post, Ledger said it was aware of a security incident impacting Optimizely, a third-party service provider used by many other sites as well.

We are aware of a security incident affecting Optimizely, a third-party service used on https://t.co/d2pWxdG49X, alongside numerous other websites. Our team has remediated the issue, and the malicious code is no longer being served through our website. This incident does not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices. Your private keys remain protected by your Ledger device. For more information from Optimizely: https://t.co/CxzmBxYadb

Website optimization platform Optimizely said it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Optimizely stated that the vulnerable path has now been blocked, the injected code has been removed, and customers have been contacted directly.

Along these lines, Ledger confirmed that its team had remediated the issue and that the malicious code was no longer being served through its website.

Ledger emphasizes that the incident did not affect the security architecture of Ledger devices and that user private keys remain protected by their Ledger device, thus reassuring users that the incident had not compromised the core security of its wallet products.

According to researcher Scott Helme, on November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of 178 organizations' websites across several sectors through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform. The websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger, and Peacock.

Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

The main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.
